On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Dovelos

item.title: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
item.description: arXiv:2611.31212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-resolution flood forecasting with full two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers remains computationally expensive, even on GPUs. We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois. The model is trained on SynxFlow SWE simulations of 113 historical storms observed across twelve Midwestern states (2003-2024), each under three antecedent-wetness scenarios, and can optionally be conditioned on coarse 100 m or 150 m hydrodynamic simulations. Because reverse diffusion is stochastic, every forecast is a 20-member ensemble drawn from the same trained model. Coarse conditioning reduces the four-day mean water-depth RMSE of the ensemble mean from 0.170 m to 0.054 m (100 m) and 0.048 m (150 m). The coarser 150 m conditioning also gives the best critical success index (0.839), false alarm ratio, CRPS and Brier score at lower cost, so finer conditioning does not guarantee better skill. Averaging members reduces error by 5-11% relative to a single realization, and the ensemble provides spatially explicit exceedance probabilities, although the ensembles are under-dispersive (spread-to-error ratios 0.35-0.73). On a single GPU, a four-day forecast over 26 non-overlapping patches is 7.8x, 11.0x and 16.3x faster than the 30 m simulation for the 100 m, 150 m and unconditioned configurations, and projected speedups for a 14-day forecast reach 12-49x for one member and 48-58x for 20 members. Physics-guided diffusion models are thus promising probabilistic surrogates for regional-scale flood forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Omar Sallam, David Coe, Jeremy Feinstein, Hugo Torres, Sofia Sahagun Covarrubias, Eugene Yan

item.title: LeJEPA Features Are Not Isotropic, and Should Not Be
item.description: arXiv:2611.31216v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The SIGReg term in LeJEPA regularizes features to have an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Our first result is to show that this regularizer, in practice, cannot achieve its goal. We design a modified regularizer to enforce the objective better. This leads to slightly improved performance. For example, on ImageNet-100, our modified regularizer reaches the final accuracy of SIGReg in 1.3$\times$ fewer epochs. Our second result argues that self-supervised encoders should not have isotropic Gaussian features. We show that the alignment term in LeJEPA conflicts with SIGReg, because it couples the magnitude of the features with their directions. In contrast, isotropic Gaussian features would entail independent magnitude and directions. Features obtained with LeJEPA are, in fact, not isotropic. So LeJEPA has two issues. Its regularizer is weak, and the isotropic Gaussian target is too strict. Our third result is about reformulating the isotropic Gaussian regularizer to enforce only the marginal distributions of the magnitude and direction, without enforcing independence. This leads to a simple regularization term, PolarReg, that can be optimized reliably across many different datasets, batch sizes and embedding dimensions without any hyper-parameter changes. On ImageNet-1k, our technique matches the accuracy of LeJEPA and its variants in 4.7$\times$ fewer epochs. It improves the final accuracy by 1.8 points.
item.dc:creator: Richeek Das, Pratik Chaudhari

item.title: Self-Supervised Dataset Distillation via Mutual Information Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2611.31225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses a frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. A synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only a few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Hossein Moslemi, Mahdi Beitollahi, Zhimin Mei, Jiale Cai, Bissan Ghaddar, Boyu Wang

item.title: TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
item.description: arXiv:2611.31233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test. We introduce a paired statistic that identifies directions where the two towers agree more on hard negatives than on matched pairs. Mildly attenuating these directions improves retrieval while largely preserving the gap. We arrive at this correction through weight-space programming: guided by the statistic, an LLM agent inspects both towers and writes closed-form weight edits without backpropagation. Free to edit any component, the agent improves COCO test retrieval on all 13 CLIP checkpoints and edits an output projection in 12 of the 13. We distill and refine its recurring correction into TowerBridge, a closed-form recipe motivated by a first-order analysis of the hard-negative margin. Computed in seconds from 25,000 labelled pairs, it requires no model-specific tuning and leaves the architecture and inference cost unchanged. TowerBridge improves COCO test retrieval by 16.8 RSUM and Flickr30k test retrieval by 6.6 on average across all 21 evaluated CLIP checkpoints, including 8 unseen by the agent, while limiting any drop in ImageNet zero-shot accuracy to 0.5 points. It also reduces hubness on all 21 checkpoints and improves retrieval on 4 of 5 dual encoders from other families.
item.dc:creator: Hani Alomari, Md Atabuzzaman, Chris Thomas

item.title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.31237v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.
item.dc:creator: JB Kim, Byungwoo Jeon, Kyungmin Lee, Hyeonmo Kang, Cheonbok Park, Shinyoung Joo, Jinwoo Shin, Jeonghoon Kim

item.title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
item.description: arXiv:2611.31240v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.
item.dc:creator: Seongchan Kim, Soowon Son, Sangoh Kim, Hyunah Ko, Eunbeen Hong, Hyunkoo Lee, Sanghyun Lee, WonJun Moon, Kihong Kim, Dongyeon Son, Woongchan Nam, Seungryong Kim

item.title: Personalized Execution Time Optimization for Billion-Scale Scheduled Jobs
item.description: arXiv:2203.06158v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scheduled batch jobs are widely used on asynchronous computing platforms to execute enterprise applications such as promotional notifications and candidate pre-computation for recommender systems. Delivering or updating information at the right time is important for user experience and execution impact, yet providing a versatile, personalized execution time optimization solution across diverse product scenarios while maintaining reasonable infrastructure costs remains challenging. In this paper, we present a deployed system that serves billions of users daily, combining learning-to-rank with a "best time policy" for execution time selection. We describe the four-stage evolution of our approach: from heuristic peak-hour rules, to pointwise ML-based activity pattern predictions, to a linear signal assembler with globally fixed weights, and finally to a contextual ensemble learner that produces per-user adaptive fusion weights via a neural policy network trained with listwise learning-to-rank objectives. We further report the discovery of cross-use-case cannibalization effects and introduce a coordination system to mitigate the problem. Our production experiments demonstrate measurable improvements in both execution efficiency and downstream product impact. We share deployment lessons including failure analyses and design decisions accumulated over four years of operating this system at scale. To our knowledge, this represents the first ML-based multi-tenant execution time optimization system deployed across different product domains at industrial scale.
item.dc:creator: Yang Liu, Juan Wang, Idris Malik, Zhengxing Chen, Ian Fox, Imani Mufti, Jason Sukumaran, Baokun He, Xiling Sun, Feng Liang

item.title: From Tables to Time: Extending TabPFN-v2 to Time Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2501.02945v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent progress in foundation models has enabled strong zero-shot performance for time series forecasting. In this work, we show that such capabilities can also emerge from tabular foundation models. We introduce TabPFN-TS, a simple method that treats forecasting as a tabular regression problem by combining lightweight temporal featurization with the pretrained TabPFN-v2. This formulation requires no time-series-specific pretraining and naturally supports both univariate and covariate-informed forecasting. Despite its compact size (11M parameters), TabPFN-TS achieves state-of-the-art performance on covariate-informed forecasting and competitive accuracy on univariate forecasting across the GIFT-Eval and fev-bench benchmarks. We further provide controlled analyses examining how the model interprets temporal structure, how featurization choices affect accuracy, and how forecasts change under alternative tabular backbones. Together, our results demonstrate that tabular foundation models--when paired with suitable temporal features--offer an efficient and versatile alternative for forecasting, bridging tabular and time-series learning within a unified framework. Code is available at https://github.com/PriorLabs/tabpfn-time-series.
item.dc:creator: Shi Bin Hoo, Samuel M\"uller, David Salinas, Frank Hutter

item.title: Supervised Contrastive Learning of Environment-Invariant Representations
item.description: arXiv:2502.07281v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-world datasets often combine data collected under different experimental conditions. This yields larger datasets, but can also introduce environment-associated correlations that make it difficult to model the phenomena of interest. We address this with Supervised Contrastive Invariance Learning (SCIL), which learns a task-supervised representation $z_c$ while regularizing its environment-related structure, together with an environment-supervised auxiliary representation $z_s$. The contribution of the auxiliary representation to the reported results remains unresolved. SCIL is based purely on Supervised Contrastive Learning and uses a single hyperparameter $\alpha$ to control the strength of environment regularization. We study this regularization under distribution shift with Colored MNIST and Camelyon17-WILDS, where increasing $\alpha$ decreases in-distribution validation accuracy and increases held-out test accuracy. We also evaluate SCIL on batch correction for 26 million Optical Pooled Screening images, where $z_c$ preserves biological signal while becoming less predictive of inter-well variation.
item.dc:creator: Taro Makino, Ji Won Park, Natasa Tagasovska, Takamasa Kudo, Paula Coelho, Jan-Christian Huetter, Heming Yao, Burkhard Hoeckendorf, Ana Carolina Leote, Stephen Ra, David Richmond, Kyunghyun Cho, Aviv Regev, Romain Lopez

item.title: When majority rules, minority loses: bias amplification of gradient descent
item.description: arXiv:2505.13122v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite growing empirical evidence of bias amplification in machine learning, its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. We develop a formal framework for majority-minority learning tasks, showing how standard training can favor majority groups and produce stereotypical predictors that neglect minority-specific features. Assuming population and variance imbalance, our analysis reveals three key findings: (i) the close proximity between ``full-data'' and stereotypical predictors, (ii) the dominance of a region where training the entire model tends to merely learn the majority traits, and (iii) a lower bound on the additional training required. Our results are illustrated through experiments in deep learning for tabular and image classification tasks.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: NeurIPS 2025 - Thirty-ninth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, Dec 2025, San Diego (CA), United States
item.dc:creator: Fran\c{c}ois Bachoc (LPP), J{\'e}r{\^o}me Bolte (TSE-R), Ryan Boustany (TSE-R), Jean-Michel Loubes (IMT, REGALIA)

item.title: Learn to Vaccinate: Combining Structure Learning and Effective Vaccination for Epidemic and Outbreak Control
item.description: arXiv:2506.15397v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model is a widely used model for the spread of information and infectious diseases, particularly non-immunizing ones, on a graph. Given a highly contagious disease, a natural question is how to best vaccinate individuals to minimize the disease's extinction time. While previous works showed that the problem of optimal vaccination is closely linked to the NP-hard Spectral Radius Minimization (SRM) problem, they assumed that the graph is known, which is often not the case in practice. In this work, we consider the problem of minimizing the extinction time of an outbreak modeled by an SIS model where the graph on which the disease spreads is unknown and only the infection states of the vertices are observed. To this end, we split the problem into two: learning the graph and determining effective vaccination strategies. We propose a novel inclusion-exclusion-based learning algorithm and, unlike previous approaches, establish its sample complexity for graph recovery. We then detail an optimal SRM algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the number of vertices for bounded treewidth and a fixed vaccination budget. This is complemented by an efficient and effective polynomial-time greedy heuristic for any graph. Finally, we present experiments on synthetic and real-world data that numerically validate our learning and vaccination algorithms.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
item.dc:creator: Sepehr Elahi, Paula M\"urmann, Patrick Thiran

item.title: Time-MAGNET: Federated Multimodal Graph Neural Expert Transformer for Human Activity Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2508.01701v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human Activity Recognition plays a vital role in applications such as fitness tracking, smart homes, and healthcare monitoring. Single modality HAR systems rely on a single source of sensory information and can therefore be affected by sensor specific noise and signal degradation, which may limit their ability to distinguish between activities. To address these limitations, this work proposes Time-MAGNET, a novel multimodal learning framework that adaptively fuses heterogeneous sensing modalities to learn discriminative representations for HAR. It adaptively models interactions among heterogeneous modalities using graph attention and a Mixture-of-Experts architecture. To capture complex temporal dependencies, we employ a lightweight encoder-only T5 architecture customized for multimodal HAR and efficiently trained using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). In real world applications, multimodal HAR data are typically distributed across devices or users and cannot always be centrally collected due to privacy, data ownership, and communication constraints. However, the distributed nature of HAR introduces statistical and system heterogeneity across clients, which can challenge conventional federated aggregation methods. To address this issue, we propose Federated Proximal Adaptive Weighting (FedPAW), a novel federated aggregation algorithm for stable and effective model aggregation under heterogeneous client settings. Extensive experiments on the MEx dataset show that Time-MAGNET achieves accuracies of 0.9555 and 0.8997 in centralized and federated settings, respectively, outperforming the considered baseline methods. The results indicate that adaptive multimodal fusion and LoRA based temporal modeling improve centralized HAR performance, while FedPAW provides effective aggregation under heterogeneous federated clients.
item.dc:creator: Asmit Bandyopadhyay, Tanmay Sen, Rohit Basu, Swagatam Das

item.title: SpikeSTAG: A Dendritic Compartmental Spiking Graph Network for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2508.02069v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a distinctive paradigm for temporal modeling through their intrinsic membrane potential dynamics. However, existing SNN-based forecasting methods focus exclusively on temporal processing, lacking mechanisms to capture spatial dependencies among variables. To bridge this gap, we propose SpikeSTAG, a neuromorphic spatiotemporal architecture that integrates graph-based spatial reasoning into spike-driven temporal computation. Central to our approach is the Dendritic Graph Module, which reinterprets spectral graph convolutions as biological dendritic integration --- coupling multi-scale spatial aggregation with the temporal dynamics of spiking neurons within a single computational unit. To adaptively fuse the resulting spatial and temporal representations, we further introduce a Dual-Stream Integration Module that employs competitive gating and coincidence-based amplification, selectively enhancing consistent spatiotemporal patterns while suppressing conflicting noise. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpikeSTAG establishes a new state-of-the-art among SNN-based models and surpasses representative ANN baselines, while reducing theoretical energy consumption by approximately 66.7\% compared to Transformer architectures.
item.dc:creator: Bang Hu, Changze Lv, Junyi Wang, Mingjie Li, Xiaoqing Zheng, Fan Zhang, Wei Cao

item.title: Unlearning That Lasts: Utility-Preserving, Robust, and Almost Irreversible Forgetting in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2509.02820v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Unlearning in large language models (LLMs) requires precisely removing specific information from a pre-trained model, e.g. to delete private data or harmful knowledge acquired during pre-training. However, existing unlearning methods often fall short under thorough evaluation. This paper makes three contributions. First, we introduce JensUn, a novel unlearning approach which leverages the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) as the training objective for both forget and retain sets. We provide theoretical arguments why JSD outperforms KL-Divergence, and show in extensive experiments that JensUn achieves the best forget-utility trade-off and demonstrates strong resilience to benign relearning, outperforming existing methods. Second, for a precise unlearning evaluation, we introduce LPF, a curated dataset of less prominent facts that provides a realistic unlearning scenario. Third, to comprehensively test unlearning methods, we $\textit{(i)}$ employ an LLM as semantic judge instead of the standard ROUGE score, and $\textit{(ii)}$ evaluate worst-case unlearning over various paraphrases and input formats. Our improved evaluation reveals that many unlearning methods are less effective than previously thought.
item.dc:creator: Naman Deep Singh, Maximilian M\"uller, Amit Peleg, Francesco Croce, Matthias Hein

item.title: PPGFlowECG: Latent Rectified Flow with Cross-Modal Encoding for PPG-Guided ECG Generation and Cardiovascular Disease Detection
item.description: arXiv:2509.19774v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is the clinical gold standard for cardiovascular disease (CVD) assessment, yet continuous monitoring is constrained by the need for dedicated hardware and trained personnel. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is ubiquitous in wearable devices and readily scalable, but it lacks electrophysiological specificity, limiting diagnostic reliability. While generative methods aim to translate PPG into clinically useful ECG signals, existing approaches are limited by the misalignment of physiological semantics in generative models and the complexity of modeling in high-dimensional signals. To address these limitations, we propose PPGFlowECG, a two-stage framework that aligns PPG and ECG in a shared latent space using the CardioAlign Encoder and then synthesizes ECGs with latent rectified flow. We further provide a formal analysis of this coupling, showing that the CardioAlign Encoder is necessary to guarantee stable and semantically consistent ECG synthesis under our formulation. Extensive experiments on four datasets demonstrate improved synthesis fidelity and downstream diagnostic utility. These results indicate that PPGFlowECG supports scalable, wearable-first CVD screening when standard ECG acquisition is unavailable.
item.dc:creator: Xiaocheng Fang, Jiarui Jin, Haoyu Wang, Che Liu, Jieyi Cai, Yujie Xiao, Guangkun Nie, Bo Liu, Shun Huang, Hongyan Li, Shenda Hong

item.title: Improving constraint-based discovery with robust propagation and reliable LLM priors
item.description: arXiv:2509.23570v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning causal structure from observational data is central to scientific modeling and decision-making. Constraint-based methods aim to recover conditional independence (CI) relations in a causal directed acyclic graph (DAG). Classical approaches such as PC and subsequent methods orient v-structures first and then propagate edge directions from these seeds, assuming perfect CI tests and exhaustive search of separating subsets -- assumptions often violated in practice, leading to cascading errors in the final graph. Recent work has explored using large language models (LLMs) as experts, prompting sets of nodes for edge directions, and could augment edge orientation when assumptions are not met. However, such methods implicitly assume perfect experts, which is unrealistic for hallucination-prone LLMs. We propose MosaCD, a causal discovery method that propagates edges from a high-confidence set of seeds derived from both CI tests and LLM annotations. To filter hallucinations, we introduce shuffled queries that exploit LLMs' positional bias, retaining only high-confidence seeds. We then apply a novel confidence-down propagation strategy that orients the most reliable edges first, and can be integrated with any skeleton-based discovery method. Across multiple real-world graphs, MosaCD achieves higher accuracy in final graph construction than existing constraint-based methods, largely due to the improved reliability of initial seeds and robust propagation strategies.
item.dc:creator: Ruiqi Lyu, Alistair Turcan, Martin Jinye Zhang, Bryan Wilder

item.title: Improving Sample Complexity of Critic-Actor Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2510.04189v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There has been significant research activity on studying the theoretical convergence guarantees (both asymptotic and non-asymptotic) for actor-critic (AC) algorithms. In a couple of recent papers, two-timescale critic-actor algorithms have been proposed where the role of the actor and critic is reversed, resulting in the algorithm mimicking value iteration as opposed to policy iteration. Finite time analysis has been carried out for a two-timescale critic-actor (CA) algorithm with function approximation and a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-(2+\delta)})$ is obtained for some $\delta>0$ that is a function of the separation between the two step sizes. In this paper, we obtain improved sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ that had previously been achieved only by the single-timescale actor-critic algorithm. We propose modified learning rates for the actor and critic recursions that result in the improved sample complexity of the algorithm. This we obtain after weakening a key assumption in prior work. The sample complexity we obtain is the best so far reported in the literature for any multi-scale actor-critic or critic-actor algorithm. While the single-timescale actor-critic algorithm also achieves this sample complexity, it has been pointed out in prior work that this algorithm is not guaranteed to be asymptotically stable almost surely unlike our algorithm since we use a timescale separation for the critic and the actor. We additionally fully perform a finite-time analysis of the constrained natural critic-actor algorithm using the modified learning rates and also obtain a sample complexity bound of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$. We further show the results of experiments on different Gym and Safety-Gym environments where our algorithms are found to show good performance and are competitive in comparison to other well-known algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Prashansa Panda, Shalabh Bhatnagar

item.title: Large Language Model Unlearning Under the Microscope: A Benchmark Study
item.description: arXiv:2510.07626v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine unlearning for large language models (LLMs), known as LLM unlearning, aims to remove undesired data, knowledge, and behaviors while preserving model capabilities. Despite rapid progress over the past two years, research in LLM unlearning remains fragmented, with limited clarity on what constitutes effective unlearning and how it should be rigorously evaluated. In this work, we present a principled taxonomy of twelve recent stateful unlearning methods, grouped into three methodological families: divergence-driven optimization, representation misalignment, and rejection-based targeted unlearning. Building on this taxonomy, we revisit the evaluation of unlearning effectiveness (UE), utility retention (UT), and robustness (Rob), focusing on WMDP for hazardous knowledge and associated model capability removal. Our analysis shows that current evaluations, dominated by multiple-choice question (MCQ) accuracy, offer only a narrow perspective, often overstating success while overlooking model generation behavior. To address this gap, we introduce open question answering (Open-QA) metrics to better capture generative performance and reveal the strengths and limitations of different unlearning method families. Furthermore, we demonstrate that robustness requires finer-grained analysis. For example, vulnerabilities differ substantially between in-domain relearning and out-of-domain fine-tuning, even though both fall under model-level attacks. Through this study, we provide a full-stack re-examination of LLM unlearning and actionable guidance for designing and evaluating future methods. Code and model checkpoints are publicly available on GitHub and Hugging Face.
item.dc:creator: Chongyu Fan, Changsheng Wang, Yancheng Huang, Soumyadeep Pal, Sijia Liu

item.title: When and Why Does Multi-Agent Debate Fail and Does It Really Underperform?
item.description: arXiv:2510.20963v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) was proposed as a promising approach for ensembling the wisdom of multiple large language models (LLMs) to improve reasoning and provide effective supervision to superhuman LLMs. However, increasing empirical evidence suggests that MAD may not outperform or even underperform single-agent approaches (SA), raising doubts about the benefits of MAD. In this work, we investigate this issue by analyzing the incentive structures of popular MAD paradigms: (i) competitive MAD (CopMAD) where agents compete by holding opposing positions; (ii) consensus-seeking MAD (CosMAD) where agents are driven to seek consensus. We show that both paradigms suffer from debate hacking: CopMAD reduces to a cheap-talk game, where agents produce misleading messages to win the game, while CosMAD filters out informative disagreements for premature consensus. Consequently, agents in both CopMAD and CosMAD fail to jointly resolve the ambiguity and seek the truth. To this end, we introduce ColMAD, a collaborative protocol that reframes MAD as a non-zero-sum game to encourage agents to provide informative while truthful messages. Through extensive benchmarking on challenging tasks such as error detection, we show that ColMAD consistently outperforms previous MAD protocols under multi-seed evaluation across heterogeneous LLM pairs. Under the same budgets, ColMAD effectively brings non-trivial improvements over SA methods, implying that the protocol design is critical to realizing the potential of MAD. The code is available at https://github.com/LFhase/ColMAD .
item.dc:creator: Yongqiang Chen, Gang Niu, James Cheng, Bo Han, Masashi Sugiyama

item.title: Entangled Schr\"odinger Bridge Matching
item.description: arXiv:2511.07406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulating trajectories of multi-particle systems on complex energy landscapes is a central task in molecular dynamics (MD) and drug discovery, but remains challenging at scale due to computationally expensive and long simulations. Previous approaches leverage techniques such as flow or Schr\"odinger bridge matching to implicitly learn joint trajectories from data snapshots. However, many systems, including biomolecular systems and heterogeneous cell populations, undergo dynamic interactions that evolve over their trajectory and cannot be captured through static snapshots. To close this gap, we introduce Entangled Schr\"odinger Bridge Matching (EntangledSBM), a framework that learns the first- and second-order stochastic dynamics of interacting, multi-particle systems where the direction and magnitude of each particle's path depend dynamically on the paths of the other particles. We define the Entangled Schr\"odinger Bridge (EntangledSB) problem as solving a coupled system of bias forces that entangle particle velocities. We show that our framework accurately simulates heterogeneous cell populations under perturbations and rare transitions in high-dimensional biomolecular systems.
item.dc:creator: Sophia Tang, Yinuo Zhang, Pranam Chatterjee

item.title: Transformer Semantic Genetic Programming for d-dimensional Symbolic Regression Problems
item.description: arXiv:2511.09416v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transformer Semantic Genetic Programming (TSGP) is a semantic search approach that uses a pre-trained transformer model as a variation operator to generate offspring programs with high semantic similarity to a given parent. Unlike other semantic GP approaches that rely on fixed syntactic transformations, TSGP aims to learn diverse structural variations that lead to solutions with similar semantics. We find that a single transformer model trained on millions of programs is able to generalize across symbolic regression problems of varying dimensions. Evaluated on 24 real-world and synthetic datasets, TSGP significantly outperforms standard GP, SLIM_GSGP, Deep Symbolic Regression, and Denoising Autoencoder GP, achieving an average rank of 1.58 across all benchmarks. Moreover, TSGP produces more compact solutions than SLIM_GSGP, despite its higher accuracy. In addition, the target semantic distance is able to effectively adjust the step size in the semantic space: small values enable consistent improvement in fitness but often lead to larger programs, while larger values promote faster convergence and compactness. Thus, the target semantic distance provides an effective mechanism for balancing exploration and exploitation.
item.dc:creator: Philipp Anthes, Dominik Sobania, Franz Rothlauf

item.title: Federated style aware transformer aggregation of representations
item.description: arXiv:2511.18841v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) faces persistent challenges, including domain heterogeneity from diverse client data, data imbalance due to skewed participation, and strict communication constraints. Traditional federated learning often lacks personalization, as a single global model cannot capture client-specific characteristics, leading to biased predictions and poor generalization, especially for clients with highly divergent data distributions. To address these issues, we propose FedSTAR, a style-aware federated learning framework that disentangles client-specific style factors from shared content representations. FedSTAR aggregates class-wise prototypes using a Transformer-based attention mechanism, allowing the server to adaptively weight client contributions while preserving personalization. Furthermore, by exchanging compact prototypes and style vectors instead of full model parameters, FedSTAR significantly reduces communication overhead. Experimental results demonstrate that combining content-style disentanglement with attention-driven prototype aggregation improves personalization and robustness in heterogeneous environments without increasing communication cost.
item.dc:creator: Mincheol Jeon, Euinam Huh

item.title: Average-reward reinforcement learning in semi-Markov decision processes via relative value iteration
item.description: arXiv:2512.06218v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper applies the authors' recent results on asynchronous stochastic approximation (SA) in the Borkar-Meyn framework to reinforcement learning in average-reward semi-Markov decision processes (SMDPs). We establish the convergence of an asynchronous SA analogue of Schweitzer's classical relative value iteration algorithm, RVI Q-learning, for finite-space, weakly communicating SMDPs. In particular, we show that the algorithm converges almost surely to a compact, connected subset of solutions to the average-reward optimality equation, with convergence to a unique, sample path-dependent solution under additional stepsize and asynchrony conditions. Moreover, to make full use of the SA framework, we introduce new monotonicity conditions for estimating the optimal reward rate in RVI Q-learning. These conditions substantially expand the previously considered algorithmic framework and are addressed through novel arguments in the stability and convergence analysis of RVI Q-learning.
item.dc:creator: Huizhen Yu, Yi Wan, Richard S. Sutton

item.title: Random-Bridges as Stochastic Transports for Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2512.14190v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper motivates the use of random-bridges -- stochastic processes conditioned to take target distributions at fixed timepoints -- in the realm of generative modelling. Herein, random-bridges act as stochastic transports between two probability distributions when appropriately initialized, displaying either Markovian or non-Markovian, and continuous, discontinuous, or hybrid patterns depending on the choice of the driving process. We show how one can start from general probabilistic statements and branch out into specific representations for learning and simulation algorithms. Essentially, our framework formulates stochastic transports as noisy information processes governing the dynamic translation and propagation of information between arbitrary probability measures. Our theoretical and algorithmic presentation details training and simulation frameworks for both Gaussian and L\'evy (specifically, Gamma, Poisson and Stable-$1/2$) random-bridge transports. The empirical validation focuses on the Gaussian case for demonstration and comparison purposes, where our construct delivers high-quality samples, achieving competitive Fr\'echet Inception Distance scores compared to widely used denoising diffusions and flow matching frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Goria, Levent A. Meng\"ut\"urk, Murat C. Meng\"ut\"urk, Berkan Sesen

item.title: HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni
item.description: arXiv:2601.01792v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni, the first any-to-any omnimodal model in the HyperCLOVA X family that supports text, audio, and vision as both inputs and outputs. By consolidating multimodal understanding and generation into a single model rather than separate modality-specific pipelines, HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni serves as an 8B-scale omni-pathfinding point toward practical any-to-any omni assistants. At a high level, the model unifies modalities through a shared next-token prediction interface over an interleaved multimodal sequence, while vision and audio encoders inject continuous embeddings for fine-grained understanding and grounding. Empirical evaluations demonstrate competitive performance against comparably sized models across diverse input-output combinations spanning text, audio, and vision, in both Korean and English. We anticipate that the open-weight release of HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni will support a wide range of research and deployment scenarios.
item.dc:creator: NAVER Cloud HyperCLOVA X Team

item.title: Dynamic Hyperparameter Importance for Efficient Multi-Objective Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2601.03166v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Choosing a suitable ML model is a complex task that can depend on several objectives, e.g., accuracy, fairness, or energy consumption. In practice, this requires trading off multiple, often competing, objectives through multi-objective optimization (MOO). However, existing MOO methods typically treat all hyperparameters as equally important, disregarding that hyperparameter importance (HPI) can vary significantly across objectives. We propose a novel dynamic optimization approach that prioritizes the most influential hyperparameters based on varying objective trade-offs during the search, thereby accelerating empirical convergence. We advance prior work on HPI for MOO from post-analysis to direct, dynamic integration within the optimization, using HyperSHAP, a recent HPI method that attributes performance gains to hyperparameters via Shapley values. For this, we leverage the objective weightings naturally produced by the MOO algorithm ParEGO and reduce the configuration space by fixing the unimportant hyperparameters, allowing the search to focus on the important ones. We evaluate our method on synthetic tasks from \pymoo and moderate-dimensional HPO tasks from \yahpo. For HPO, integrating HPI yields 62\% improvement in final Pareto front quality, while on synthetic data, the improvement is 71\% over standard ParEGO.
item.dc:creator: Daphne Theodorakopoulos, Marcel Wever, Marius Lindauer

item.title: Asymptotic Universal Alignment: A New Alignment Framework via Test-Time Scaling
item.description: arXiv:2601.08777v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) to serve users with heterogeneous and potentially conflicting preferences is a central challenge for personalized and trustworthy AI. We formalize an ideal notion of universal alignment through test-time scaling: for each prompt, the model produces $k\ge 1$ candidate responses and a user selects their preferred one. We introduce $(k,f(k))$-robust alignment, which requires the $k$-output model to have win rate $f(k)$ against any other single-output model, and asymptotic universal alignment (U-alignment), which requires $f(k)\to 1$ as $k\to\infty$. Our main result characterizes the optimal convergence rate: there exists a family of single-output policies whose $k$-sample product policies achieve U-alignment at rate $f(k)=\frac{k}{k+1}$, and no method can achieve a faster rate in general. We show that popular post-training methods, including Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF), can fundamentally underutilize the benefits of test-time scaling. Even though NLHF is optimal for $k=1$, sampling from the resulting (often deterministic) policy cannot guarantee win rates above $\tfrac{1}{2}$ except for an arbitrarily small slack. This stems from a lack of output diversity: existing alignment methods can collapse to a single majority-preferred response, making additional samples redundant. In contrast, our approach preserves output diversity and achieves the optimal test-time scaling rate. In particular, we propose a family of symmetric multi-player alignment games and prove that any symmetric Nash equilibrium policy of the $(k+1)$-player alignment game achieves the optimal $(k,\frac{k}{k+1})$-robust alignment. Finally, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees for self-play learning dynamics in these games and extend the framework to opponents that also generate multiple responses.
item.dc:creator: Yang Cai, Weiqiang Zheng

item.title: Calibration without Ground Truth
item.description: arXiv:2601.19862v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a label-free post-processing framework that improves a strong but miscalibrated primary model using a weaker yet better-calibrated reference. Our key insight is that strict worst-case improvement is possible if and only if the two models are not mutually calibrated, meaning there does not exist a joint distribution over their reports and outcomes such that both predictions are simultaneously calibrated. We formalize this condition and connect it to no-arbitrage results from economics. Under this condition, we develop an efficient post-processing algorithm for the strong model's outputs based on Bregman projection, with a strict worst-case performance improvement guarantee. Experiments on three 8B LLM families across three multiple-choice benchmarks show that our method reduces the primary model's ECE by over $40\%$ on common benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Yuqing Kong, Mingyu Song, Yizhou Wang, Yifan Wu

item.title: Zenith: Scaling up Ranking Models for Billion-scale Livestreaming Recommendation
item.description: arXiv:2601.21285v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurately capturing feature interactions is essential in recommender systems, and recent trends show that scaling up model capacity could be a key driver for next-level predictive performance. While prior work has explored various model architectures to capture multi-granularity feature interactions, relatively little attention has been paid to efficient feature handling and scaling model capacity without incurring excessive inference latency. In this paper, we address this challenge by presenting Zenith, a scalable and efficient ranking architecture that learns complex feature interactions with minimal runtime overhead. Zenith uses Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) as a common capacity-scaling mechanism across feature interaction and long-sequence encoding, while adapting its parameterization to each token regime. The Feature Interaction Unit applies tokenwise attention and SMoE to a small, fixed set of high-dimensional Prime Tokens. In contrast, the Sequence Encoding Unit processes thousands of temporal tokens with SMoE-based query, key, and value projections and an SMoE-based feed-forward network. For the livestreaming-specific delayed-feedback problem, Zenith's Target Modeling Unit efficiently connects timely but incomplete short-horizon supervision with complete long-horizon supervision. Its real-world effectiveness is demonstrated through deployment on TikTok Live, a leading online livestreaming platform that attracts billions of users globally. Our online A/B test achieves gains of 9.93% in Quality Watch Session / User and 8.11% in Quality Watch Duration / User.
item.dc:creator: Ruifeng Zhang, Zexi Huang, Zikai Wang, Ke Sun, Bohang Zheng, Yuchen Jiang, Zhe Chen, Zhen Ouyang, Huimin Xie, Phil Shen, Junlin Zhang, Yuchao Zheng, Wentao Guo, Qinglei Wang

item.title: More Bang for the Buck: Improving the Inference of Large Language Models at a Fixed Budget using Reset and Discard (ReD)
item.description: arXiv:2601.21522v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The performance of large language models (LLMs) on verifiable tasks is usually measured by pass@k, the probability of solving a problem correctly at least once in k trials. At a fixed budget, a more suitable metric is coverage@cost, the average number of unique problems solved as a function of the total number of attempts. We connect the two metrics and show that the empirically-observed power-law behavior in pass@k leads to a sublinear growth of the coverage@cost (diminishing returns). To solve this problem, we propose Reset-and-Discard (ReD), a query method of LLMs that increases coverage@cost for a given budget, regardless of the pass@k form. Moreover, given a pass@k, we can quantitatively predict the savings in the total number of attempts using ReD. If pass@k is not available for the model, ReD can infer its power-law exponent. Experiments across coding (HumanEval), math (GSM8K), and reasoning (MMLU-Pro) benchmarks, as well as real GitHub issues solved by a coding agent (SWE-bench Lite), demonstrate that ReD substantially reduces the required attempts, tokens, and USD cost to reach a desired coverage, while also offering an efficient way to measure inference power-laws. ReD's advantage is maintained for imperfect verifiers.
item.dc:creator: Sagi Meir, Tommer D. Keidar, Noam Levi, Shlomi Reuveni, Barak Hirshberg

item.title: Beyond Forgetting: Representation Misdirection Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
item.description: arXiv:2601.21702v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider Representation Misdirection (RM), a simple unlearning mechanism for large language models (LLMs) that achieves unlearning by redirecting the latent representations of forget samples toward a target vector. Despite being important, the role of the target vector used in RM remains insufficiently explored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH). Specifically, if one can identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the LRH enables linear operations on this concept vector within the representation space of the forget samples. From this perspective, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning via RM elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. We empirically validate this hypothesis across a wide range of concepts and tasks, including controlling unlearned models' truthfulness, sentiment, stereotypical bias, refusal, language, and instruction-following. Our findings reveal that this phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing unlearned models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.
item.dc:creator: Tien Dang, The-Hai Nguyen, Dinh Mai Phuong, Nguyen Minh Phuong, Anh Bui, Hoang Thanh-Tung, Le-Minh Nguyen, Naoya Inoue

item.title: From Inexact Gradients to Byzantine Robustness: Acceleration and Optimization under Similarity
item.description: arXiv:2602.03329v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distributed learning algorithms are vulnerable to adversarial nodes, a.k.a. Byzantine failures. To solve this issue, robust algorithms have been developed, which typically replace parameter averaging with robust aggregations. While generic conditions on these aggregations exist to guarantee the convergence of (Stochastic) Gradient Descent (SGD), the analyses remain rather ad hoc. This hinders the development of more complex robust algorithms, such as accelerated ones. In this work, we show that Byzantine-robust distributed optimization can, under standard generic assumptions, be cast as a general optimization with inexact gradient oracles, an active field of research. This allows us to obtain state-of-the-art results for Byzantine-robust optimization from general inexact first-order analyses. We first show that inexact GD on top of standard robust aggregation procedures obtains optimal asymptotic error in the Byzantine setting. Going further, we study an algorithm for Optimization under Similarity, in which the server leverages an auxiliary loss function that approximates the global loss. Then, we introduce an Accelerated Extra-gradient method that yields acceleration in both the standard and similarity settings. We first give new general convergence results for these inexact schemes, improving the tolerance level of acceleration to a relative error term by a $\kappa^{1/2}$ factor over previous analysis, and then instantiate these results in the Byzantine setting through our reduction. Both algorithms drastically reduce the communication complexity, as we show theoretically and empirically.
item.dc:creator: Renaud Gaucher, Aymeric Dieuleveut, Hadrien Hendrikx

item.title: Shiva-DiT: Residual-Based Differentiable Top-$k$ Selection for Efficient Diffusion Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2602.05605v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are costly at high resolution because self-attention scales quadratically with token sequence length. Existing pruning methods do not jointly provide end-to-end learnability, low training overhead, and deterministic token counts for predictable token-dependent computation. We propose Shiva-DiT, based on Residual-Based Differentiable Top-k Selection. Its forward pass executes hard top-k selection, while a residual-aware straight-through estimator propagates gradients to both token scores and the budget k without evaluating a second backbone path. A Context-Aware Router and Adaptive Ratio Policy learn layer- and timestep-dependent retention schedules under a target average budget. Experiments on SD3-Medium, Flux.1-dev, and PixArt-{\Sigma} show consistent reductions in FLOPs and measured latency. On SD3-Medium, Shiva-DiT provides four fidelity-latency operating points and reaches a 1.54x wall-clock speedup with competitive fidelity.
item.dc:creator: Jiaji Zhang, Hailiang Zhao, Jiaju Wu, Ruichao Sun, Xinkui Zhao, Shuiguang Deng

item.title: On the Convergence of Multicalibration Gradient Boosting
item.description: arXiv:2602.06773v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multicalibration gradient boosting has recently emerged as a scalable method that empirically produces approximately multicalibrated predictors and has been deployed at web scale. Despite this empirical success, its convergence properties are not well understood. In this paper, we provide computational guarantees for multicalibration gradient boosting algorithms. We show that the magnitude of successive prediction updates decays at $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ (in the minimum over $T$ rounds), which implies the same convergence rate bound for the empirical multicalibration error over rounds. For the squared-error loss, this rate improves to linear convergence under additional smoothness assumptions on the weak learners, and convergence extends to relaxed and adaptive rescaling variants. Combining the empirical bound with uniform convergence arguments, we also bound the population multicalibration error for the log-loss under additional conditions on the weak learners, which yields a prescription for the number of rounds as a function of the sample size. Experiments on real-world datasets support our theory, clarify the regimes in which the method achieves fast convergence, and show that early stopping is needed on held-out data.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Haimovich, Fridolin Linder, Lorenzo Perini, Niek Tax, Milan Vojnovic

item.title: Efficient Adaptive Data Analysis over Dense Data Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2602.07732v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern data workflows are inherently adaptive, repeatedly querying the same dataset to refine and validate sequential decisions, but such adaptivity can lead to overfitting and invalid statistical inference. Adaptive Data Analysis (ADA) mechanisms address this challenge; however, there is a fundamental tension between computational efficiency and sample complexity. For $T$ rounds of adaptive analysis, computationally efficient algorithms typically incur suboptimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ sample complexity, whereas for arbitrary distributions, algorithms with $O(\log T)$ sample complexity are computationally intractable under standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work, we shed light on this trade-off by identifying a natural class of data distributions under which both computational efficiency and logarithmic sample complexity in $T$ are achievable. We propose a computationally efficient ADA mechanism that attains $O(\log T)$ sample complexity, optimal in its dependence on $T$, when the data distribution is dense with respect to a known prior. This setting includes, in particular, feature-label data distributions arising in distribution-specific learning. As a consequence, our mechanism also yields a sample-efficient (i.e., $O(\log T)$ samples) statistical query oracle in the distribution-specific setting. Moreover, although our algorithm is not based on differential privacy, it satisfies a relaxed privacy notion known as Predicate Singling Out (PSO) security (Cohen and Nissim 2020) whenever the number of its possible update transcripts is polynomial in the sample size. Our results thus reveal an inherent connection between adaptive data analysis and privacy beyond differential privacy.
item.dc:creator: Joon Suk Huh

item.title: RAM-Net: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Sparsely Addressable State
item.description: arXiv:2602.11958v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Linear attention offers an efficient alternative to full attention with a fixed-size recurrent state. However, this state is shared by all tokens, so information from distinct tokens becomes superposed within it and produces inter-token interference that degrades long-range fine-grained recall. To address this issue, we propose RAM-Net, which replaces dense access to a shared state with sparse address-based access. RAM-Net organizes the recurrent state as a fixed-size array of independent slots and uses an Address Decoder that maps each key or query into a sparse address, selecting a small subset of slots to write to or read from at each step. This design directs tokens with non-overlapping addresses to disjoint slots, suppressing inter-token interference, while keeping per-step state access dependent only on the number of selected slots rather than the total state size. Empirically, RAM-Net outperforms strong recurrent baselines on fine-grained long-range retrieval and achieves the lowest perplexity with competitive commonsense reasoning. It does so while accessing fewer state elements per step than all baselines, e.g., $8\times$ fewer than Mamba2.
item.dc:creator: Kaicheng Xiao, Haotian Li, Liran Dong, Guoliang Xing

item.title: Econometric vs. Causal structure learning for time-series data: Implications for policy interventions using COVID-19 data
item.description: arXiv:2603.00041v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study compares regression-based and causal structure-learning approaches to recovering temporal dependencies in UK COVID-19 data and assesses their suitability for policy analysis. We evaluate four econometric methods and eleven structure-learning algorithms using a common lag-expanded dataset that permits edges only from past to current variables. The dataset comprises 866 daily observations and 45 variables, represented by 55 numeric series after categorical encoding. Maximum lags of 1, 7, 14, 17 and 21 days are examined; all four econometric methods and ten structure-learning algorithms successfully return structures at every lag specification. We compare graph structure, complexity, fit and temporal-edge stability across lag specifications. The resulting graphs vary substantially in density, complexity, fit and stability. Agreement with the knowledge graph is limited, while low structural Hamming distance sometimes reflects sparsity rather than recovery of known relationships. Edge recurrence also varies markedly by method, revealing sensitivity to the allowed history window. Diagnostics for VAR models using all lagged predictors indicate residual dependence, non-normality and instability; estimation becomes infeasible at longer lag orders. Policy evaluation raises further concerns: few mobility-to-infection links emerge, few meet the empirical coverage criterion, and none do so in longer-lag analyses. Common temporal constraints therefore do not resolve methodological disagreement. Learnt dependency structures should not be treated as policy-ready causal models without stronger identification assumptions, robustness checks and sufficient empirical support for the interventions assessed.
item.dc:creator: Bruno Petrungaro, Anthony C. Constantinou

item.title: Guidance Ends When Reading Ends: Retrieval-Gated Attention Guidance for Diffusion Models through a Hopfield Lens
item.description: arXiv:2603.02531v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Beyond classifier-free guidance, attention-space guidance extrapolates between a strong and a weak attention map within a single forward pass. However, two questions that govern its behavior remain unexamined: along which direction the extrapolation should proceed, and for how many sampling steps it should be applied. The first governs sample quality, and the second governs cost. Interestingly, viewing attention as sparse Hopfield retrieval answers both questions. At every sampling step, the informative direction is the component of the residual parallel to the sparse retrieval output. The guidance acts on the prompt in proportion to the attention mass that image queries assign to text tokens; and since the prompt shapes the image only in the early part of sampling, guidance matters only while the prompt is still being read. Building on this analysis, we propose Retrieval-Gated Attention Guidance (ReGA), which extrapolates only along this parallel component and applies the update only over the early steps holding half of the total prompt-attention mass. Extensive measurements inside the attention layers of UNet and MM-DiT backbones confirm both theoretical predictions. Across various backbone models, in multi-step and few-step regimes, ReGA consistently improves text alignment and human-preference scores over existing attention-space guidance methods, while adding as little as 2% inference time on MM-DiT backbones.
item.dc:creator: Kwanyoung Kim

item.title: Actor-Accelerated Policy Dual Averaging for Reinforcement Learning in Continuous Action Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2603.10199v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Policy Dual Averaging (PDA) offers a principled Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) framework that more naturally admits value function approximation than standard PMD, enabling the use of approximate advantage (or Q-) functions while retaining strong convergence guarantees. However, applying PDA in continuous state and action spaces remains computationally challenging, since action selection involves solving an optimization subproblem at each decision step. In this paper, we propose \textit{actor-accelerated PDA} (AA-PDA), which uses a learned policy network to approximate the solution of the optimization subproblems, significantly reducing runtime. We provide a theoretical analysis that quantifies how actor approximation error impacts the convergence of PDA under suitable assumptions. We then evaluate its performance on several benchmarks in robotics, control, and operations research problems. AA-PDA achieves better performance compared to on-policy baselines such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Overall, our results take a step toward bridging the gap between the theoretical advantages of PDA and its practical deployment in continuous-action problems with function approximation. Our code is available at https://github.com/jgioa/pdarl
item.dc:creator: Ji Gao, Caleb Ju, Guanghui Lan, Zhaohui Tong

item.title: Neural Field Thermal Tomography: A Differentiable Physics Framework for Non-Destructive Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2603.11045v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inverse problems for stiff parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs), such as the inverse heat conduction problem (IHCP), are severely ill-posed: the forward map rapidly damps high-frequency interior structure before it reaches the boundary. Soft-constrained physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which embed the PDE as a residual penalty, decouple the diffusivity from the surface data in their standard two-network inverse formulation, and the evaluated variants fit boundary measurements while leaving the interior field essentially untouched. We propose Neural Field Thermal Tomography (NeFTY), a hard-constrained neural field framework for label-free three-dimensional inverse heat conduction. NeFTY represents the unknown diffusivity as a continuous coordinate-based neural network, and at every optimization step passes the candidate field through a differentiable implicit-Euler heat solver with harmonic-mean interface flux, so that the simulated temperature satisfies the discretized heat equation up to the solver tolerance. Adjoint gradients propagate the surface reconstruction error back to the network weights at solver-level memory cost, making test-time inversion tractable on a single GPU. Across synthetic 3D benchmarks, NeFTY outperforms soft-constrained PINN variants, a voxel-grid baseline, and classical L-BFGS voxel inversion through the same solver on label-free volumetric recovery, and it transfers to real thermography data, surpassing classical signal-processing baselines in both defect segmentation and depth estimation. Additional details at https://cab-lab-princeton.github.io/nefty/
item.dc:creator: Tao Zhong, Yixun Hu, Dongzhe Zheng, Aditya Sood, Christine Allen-Blanchette

item.title: Dataset Distillation Efficiently Encodes Low-Dimensional Representations from Gradient-Based Learning of Non-Linear Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2603.14830v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dataset distillation, a training-aware data compression technique, has recently attracted increasing attention as an effective tool for mitigating costs of optimization and data storage. However, progress remains largely empirical. Mechanisms underlying the extraction of task-relevant information from the training process and the efficient encoding of such information into synthetic data points remain elusive. In this paper, we theoretically analyze practical algorithms of dataset distillation applied to the gradient-based training of two-layer neural networks with width $L$. By focusing on a non-linear task structure called multi-index model, we prove that the low-dimensional structure of the problem is efficiently encoded into the resulting distilled data. This dataset reproduces a model with high generalization ability for a required memory complexity of $\tilde{\Theta}$$(r^2d+L)$, where $d$ and $r$ are the input and intrinsic dimensions of the task. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first theoretical works that include a specific task structure, leverage its intrinsic dimensionality to quantify the compression rate and study dataset distillation implemented solely via gradient-based algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Yuri Kinoshita, Naoki Nishikawa, Taro Toyoizumi

item.title: Escaping Offline Pessimism: Vector-Field Reward Shaping for Safe Frontier Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2603.18326v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While offline reinforcement learning provides reliable policies for real-world deployment, its inherent pessimism severely restricts an agent's ability to explore and collect novel data online. Drawing inspiration from safe reinforcement learning, exploring near the boundary of regions well covered by the offline dataset and reliably modeled by the simulator allows an agent to take manageable risks--venturing into informative but moderate-uncertainty states while remaining close enough to familiar regions for safe recovery. However, naively rewarding this boundary-seeking behavior can lead to a degenerate parking behavior, where the agent simply stops once it reaches the frontier. To solve this, we propose a novel vector-field reward shaping paradigm designed to induce continuous, safe boundary exploration for non-adaptive deployed policies. Operating on an uncertainty oracle trained from offline data, our reward combines two complementary components: a gradient-alignment term that attracts the agent toward a target uncertainty level, and a rotational-flow term that promotes motion along the local tangent plane of the uncertainty manifold. Through theoretical analysis, we show that this reward structure naturally induces sustained exploratory behavior along the boundary while preventing degenerate solutions. Empirically, by integrating our proposed reward shaping with Soft Actor-Critic on a 2D continuous navigation task, we validate that agents successfully traverse uncertainty boundaries while balancing safe, informative data collection with primary task completion.
item.dc:creator: Amirhossein Roknilamouki, Arnob Ghosh, Eylem Ekici, Ness B. Shroff

item.title: Informed Machine Learning with Knowledge Landmarks
item.description: arXiv:2604.00256v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Informed Machine Learning (ML) aims to improve prediction by using both data and prior knowledge. In scientific and engineering applications, accurate measurements may occupy only a small operating region of the input space, whereas available knowledge is global, coarse, and not expressed as equations. Existing physics-informed methods embed governing equations, residuals, simulators, operators, or mathematically specified constraints. However, they do not directly address learning from localized numeric data together with non-equational knowledge. We develop a Knowledge-Data (KD) ML framework for this setting. The KD-model represents coarse global knowledge as input-output information granules, termed knowledge landmarks. The method uses a landmark-guided objective that converts these landmarks into differentiable compatibility terms and balances them against local data fitting through a trade-off parameter $\lambda$. Experiments on two physics-based benchmarks show that the KD-model predicts more accurately across the full domain than a model trained on the local data alone. For most observation windows, the gain holds over a broad range of $\lambda$. The advantage persists when the sample size or label noise changes, with $\lambda$ re-selected without full-domain labels. These results show that approximate expert knowledge can guide training when dense labels or explicit equations are unavailable.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence, early access, Nov. 19, 2026
item.dc:creator: Chuyi Dai, Witold Pedrycz, Suping Xu, Ding Liu, Lin Shang, Xianmin Wang

item.title: Assessing the Performance-Efficiency Trade-off of Foundation Models in Probabilistic Electricity Price Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2604.14739v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large-scale renewable deployment adds volatility to electricity prices. Probabilistic forecasts that quantify this uncertainty support trading, dispatch, and risk management, but it remains unclear which models produce the best forecasts for probabilistic electricity price forecasting (PEPF). Time series foundation models (TSFMs) promise strong performance without task-specific training, whereas task-specific deep learning models remain standard. We compare 4 models for day-ahead PEPF in European bidding zones: NHITS with quantile regression averaging (NHITS+QRA), a Transformer- conditioned normalizing flow, and 2 TSFMs, namely Moirai and ChronosX. Models are compared using proper scoring rules, namely the continuous ranked probability score and the energy score, together with calibration diagnostics. When fine-tuned on prices and calendar features alone, the TSFMs attain the best accuracy and calibration. However, a well-configured NHITS+QRA closes most of this gap with roughly 3 orders of magnitude fewer parameters. It is the only model that converts additional exogenous feature groups, such as load, generation mix, and cross-border flows, into improved accuracy, whereas Moirai degrades markedly when given the same groups. When models are instead pretrained on 14 neighboring bidding zones and adapted to DE-LU with limited target data, NHITS+QRA reaches parity with ChronosX, consumes roughly 1 order of magnitude less training energy than Moirai, and attains the lowest expected calibration error. The ranking of TSFMs and task-specific models therefore depends on the available features and the adaptation regime. As our comparison rests on single-seed runs on one target zone, we report these rankings as indicative. We recommend weighing computational cost against marginal gains when selecting a PEPF model.
item.dc:creator: Jan Niklas Lettner, Hadeer El Ashhab, Veit Hagenmeyer, Benjamin Sch\"afer

item.title: The Override Gap: A Magnitude Account of Knowledge Conflict Failure in Hypernetwork-Based Instant LLM Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2604.23750v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hypernetwork-based methods such as Doc-to-LoRA internalize a document into an LLM's weights in a single forward pass, but struggle when the document contradicts pretraining knowledge. We study this override gap through the competition between the pretrained answer margin and the shift induced by the generated adapter. On 194 Gemma conflicts, baseline accuracy falls from 65.3% in the weakest-prior quartile to 16.3% in the strongest. We introduce two training-free methods: Selective Layer Boosting (SLB), which scales the adapter at its highest-activity layers, and Conflict-Aware Internalization (CA), which chooses between standard and stronger adaptation using a short base-model probe. Strong boosting raises Gemma deep-conflict accuracy from 46.4% to 71.0%, with conflict gains also observed on Mistral-7B and Qwen-4B. Matched-norm controls show that both update magnitude and allocation matter: SLB benefits from the generated layer and direction structure, while global scaling is competitive at the same increment budget. CA offers a workload-dependent recall-latency tradeoff, reaching 98.4% novel recall on Gemma while retaining the strong path's conflict accuracy. KID-Bench provides 486 questions spanning novel recall, mixed knowledge, and prior-graded conflicts, with answer-level semantic evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Shuaizhi Cheng, Xiang Shi, Zhiwei Zhang, Mingwei Li

item.title: Polynomial-Time Optimal Group Selection via the Double-Commutator Eigenvalue Problem
item.description: arXiv:2605.00834v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The algebraic diversity framework generalizes temporal averaging over multiple observations to algebraic group action on a single observation for second-order statistical estimation. The central open problem in this framework is $\textit{group selection}$: given an $M$-dimensional observation with unknown covariance structure, find the finite group whose spectral decomposition best matches the covariance. Naive enumeration of all subgroups of the symmetric group $S_M$ requires exponential time in $M$. We prove that this combinatorial problem, restricted to a basis of $d$ candidate generators, reduces to a generalized eigenvalue problem derived from the double commutator of the covariance matrix, with complexity $O(d^2M^2 + d^3)$ for sparse (permutation-type) generators and $O(d^2M^3 + d^3)$ in general. The minimum eigenvector gives the optimal generator in the span of the basis in closed form, with no iterative optimization. The minimum eigenvalue is zero if and only if a generator in the span commutes exactly with the covariance, and its magnitude is a certifiable optimality gap otherwise. The problem does not appear in the standard catalog of Garey and Johnson (1979) and links group theory, matrix analysis, and statistical estimation. We relate it to independent component analysis (JADE), structured matrix nearness, and simultaneous diagonalization, and show that the double-commutator form is the unique objective, up to scale, built from a unitarily invariant quadratic norm of the commutator. We extend the framework to non-Abelian symmetry recovery via a Sequential GEVP with deflation, which is sound but not always complete, give canonical generator sets whose direct testing is complete for five named group families, and add two identifiability theorems on the commutant-lattice ambiguity and on whether $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbf{R})$ recovers a generative subgroup or only a supergroup.
item.dc:creator: Mitchell A. Thornton

item.title: Breaking the Computational Barrier: Provably Efficient Actor-Critic for Low-Rank MDPs
item.description: arXiv:2605.01242v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a fundamental framework for sequential decision-making, in which an agent learns an optimal policy through interactions with an unknown environment. In settings with function approximation, many existing RL algorithms achieve favorable sample complexity, but often rely on computationally intractable oracles. In this paper, we use supervised learning as a computational proxy to establish a clear hierarchy of commonly adopted RL oracles under low-rank Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). This hierarchy shows that policy evaluation is the most computationally efficient oracle, provided that supervised learning can be efficiently solved. Motivated by this observation, we propose a novel optimistic actor-critic algorithm that relies solely on a truncated policy evaluation oracle. We prove that our algorithm outperforms the existing sample complexity guarantees for low-rank MDPs, while avoiding computationally expensive planning or optimization oracles commonly assumed in prior works. We further demonstrate that approximately low-rank MDPs capture a broad class of real world environments. Finally, we evaluate a practical variant of our algorithm with experiments on several standard Gym benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Ruiquan Huang, Donghao Li, Yingbin Liang, Jing Yang

item.title: AI Alignment via Incentives and Correction
item.description: arXiv:2605.01643v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study AI alignment through the lens of law-and-economics models of deterrence and enforcement, which treats misconduct as a rational response to incentivizes, where actors weigh the expected gain from aligning against the expected loss from being caught. We argue that the same logic arises naturally in foundational language models: an agent trained by RLHF can be modeled as deriving intrinsic reward from producing a persuasive yet incorrect response, while an auditor can be viewed as balancing monitoring (which incurs some cost) against identifying solver misalignment. Therefore, alignment can be viewed as a mechanism design problem, where stronger penalties can deter solver misbehavior but also reduce auditing pressure. Under this framework, we can characterize misalignment as an adversarial post-training problem. While standard post-training optimizes against a stationary reward signal, our mechanism constantly adapts to mitigate reward hacking against a fixed monitor. We formalize this interaction as follows: a principal (e.g., a human) defines a value function over joint alignment outcomes, and a meta-optimizer adaptively chooses granular rewards for the solver and auditor to optimize the principal's value.
